title: COUNT: how many rows are there?

steps.title: COUNT(*) - the crowd counter
steps.task: Fill the blank with the word for counting.
hints: The star inside the brackets means 'every row'.
The word starts with 'c'.
It's the same word as the title of this lesson.
Replace ___ with count.

steps.title: Count with a filter
steps.prompt:
COUNT combines beautifully with WHERE.
Ask: 'how many customers live in Marrakech?'
steps.task: Try typing: SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE city = 'Marrakech';
hints: Start with SELECT count(*) FROM customers.
Add WHERE city = …
Wrap Marrakech in single quotes.
Type: SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE city = 'Marrakech';
steps.expected_sql: SELECT count(*) FROM customers WHERE city = 'Marrakech';
steps.memory_trick: WHERE narrows first, COUNT counts what's left.

steps.title: Predict the count
steps.task: How many items were sold in pairs or more?
hints: Run the query - prediction lets you verify.
quantity >= 2 keeps rows where the number is 2, 3, 4…
It's between 60 and 80.
Answer: 70.

steps.title: NULL's little secret
steps.prompt:
COUNT(*) counts every row, even ones with empty bits.
COUNT(name) counts rows where name is NOT empty.
An empty bit is called NULL (say 'null': nothing there).
steps.task: In SQL, COUNT(name) skips rows where name is …
hints: It skips rows where the column has no value.
The special SQL word is four letters.
It looks like a mix of 'nil' and 'null'.
Answer: NULL.
steps.memory_trick: COUNT(column) skips NULLs; COUNT(*) skips nothing.

steps.title: Count the two-or-more
steps.prompt: Put it together for real - count the sale_items sold in pairs or more:
steps.task: Try typing: SELECT count(*) FROM sale_items WHERE quantity >= 2;
hints: Start with SELECT count(*).
Add FROM sale_items.
Finish with WHERE quantity >= 2.
Type: SELECT count(*) FROM sale_items WHERE quantity >= 2;
steps.expected_sql: SELECT count(*) FROM sale_items WHERE quantity >= 2;
steps.memory_trick: count + where = 'how many rows pass the filter?'
